saints: People whose work made this map knowable
Candles stay on this phone. Nothing here is sent anywhere.
Public access to research and court records · 1986–2013
Scout: “Aaron spent his short life opening up knowledge that sat behind paywalls. I keep his name close.”

At 14, Aaron was part of the working group that wrote RSS 1.0, an early version of the web-feed format. In 2008 he downloaded about 2.7 million federal court records from PACER, the courts’ paid records system; federal prosecutors brought no charges. In 2011 federal prosecutors charged him over downloading academic articles from JSTOR at MIT, with a possible sentence of up to 35 years, and later charges raised it further. He died by suicide in January 2013, at 26, before the case went to trial.
Scout: “Much of this desk got easier to name after 2013, because of Edward. I think of him every time I draw it.”

Edward was an NSA contractor. In June 2013 he gave journalists, among them Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras and Ewen MacAskill, documents describing programs like PRISM, which collected data from the biggest email and cloud companies. The US charged him under the Espionage Act and revoked his passport. He has lived in exile in Russia ever since.
The Guardian (2013): Edward Snowden, the whistleblower behind the NSA surveillance revelations
The Guardian (2013): NSA Prism program taps in to user data of Apple, Google and others
Scout: “Mark was a technician who knew what the wires in that room were for, and said so. Quiet work, and brave.”

Mark worked at AT&T for more than 22 years, his last years in San Francisco. In 2006 he brought the Electronic Frontier Foundation evidence that AT&T was routing copies of internet traffic into a secret room there controlled by the NSA: Room 641A. His documents were key evidence in EFF’s lawsuit, Hepting v. AT&T. In 2008 Congress gave the phone companies retroactive immunity, and the case was dismissed. He died in March 2025, at 79.
EFF (2025): In Memoriam: Mark Klein, AT&T whistleblower who revealed NSA mass spying
Scout: “Phil gave strong encryption to anyone who wanted it. The locks on these doors are cousins of his.”

In 1991 Phil released PGP, strong email encryption anyone could use, and published its source code. At the time US export rules treated strong encryption software as a munition, and he spent three years under criminal investigation. MIT Press printed the source code as a book, and the case was dropped in 1996 without charges.
Scout: “Daniel showed the country the Pentagon’s own secret history of the war, and spent the rest of his life standing beside the next ones.”

Daniel was a military analyst at RAND. In 1971 he gave the Pentagon Papers, a secret history of US decisions in the Vietnam War, to The New York Times, The Washington Post and other papers. He was charged under the Espionage Act, and in 1973 a judge dismissed every charge because of government misconduct, including a break-in at his psychiatrist’s office. He spoke up for later whistleblowers until his death in 2023, at 92.
US National Archives: the Pentagon Papers
The Iraq and Afghanistan war logs · born 1987
Scout: “Chelsea paid for what the public got to know with years of her life. She’s still here, and still speaking out.”

Chelsea was an Army intelligence analyst in Iraq. In 2010 she gave WikiLeaks the Iraq and Afghanistan war logs and hundreds of thousands of diplomatic cables. She was arrested that year and in 2013 sentenced to 35 years. In January 2017 President Obama commuted her sentence, after nearly seven years in confinement.
Scout: “Thomas tried every proper door first. That counts for a lot with me.”

Thomas was a senior executive at the NSA. He raised concerns about waste in a program called Trailblazer with his bosses, the inspectors general and the intelligence committees in Congress, and later spoke with a reporter. In 2010 he was indicted under the Espionage Act. In 2011 all ten charges were dropped; he pleaded to one misdemeanor and got probation, and the judge called it ‘unconscionable’ to bring such heavy charges and then drop them on the eve of trial.
Scout: “Bill built a system that kept Americans’ names locked unless a court said otherwise. Privacy can be designed in. He showed how.”

Bill spent more than 30 years at the NSA and served as a technical director. His team’s system, ThinThread, encrypted Americans’ identifying details and needed a court order to unlock them. He retired in October 2001 and joined a 2002 complaint to the Defense Department’s inspector general. In 2007 FBI agents raided his home. He was never charged.
Carried the Snowden documents out to the public · born 1964
Scout: “Laura kept the camera steady while the story was still dangerous to tell. Because of her, you can watch it happen.”

Laura is a documentary filmmaker, and was one of the first journalists to meet Edward Snowden in Hong Kong in 2013. She reported on the documents and made Citizenfour, which won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. Before any of that, by her own account, she had been stopped and questioned at US borders on dozens of trips.

Security researchers traced Aurora to Elderwood, a Beijing-based group with ties to China’s military. NSO Group sells Pegasus to government agencies.

These go around the locks: into the phone or laptop itself, or into the company. The CIA’s phone and computer hacking tools were exposed in the Vault 7 leak (2017). Beyond your control. For people at higher risk, Google’s Advanced Protection Program requires a passkey or security key to sign in and is stricter about risky downloads.

Apple holds this data, so an agency that wants it asks Apple, not you. One setting changes this floor: Advanced Data Protection end-to-end encrypts your backups, photos, iCloud Drive and notes, so Apple can’t hand those over. It doesn’t cover iCloud Mail, contacts or calendars. The rest is here so you know exactly who can ask, and with what.
Subpoena · 2703(d) court order · search warrant · emergency request
State police and prosecutors use the same tools.

A subpoena gets Apple to hand over your name, address, email address and phone number, and iCloud connection logs with IP addresses (kept up to 25 days). A 2703(d) court order adds your mail logs: who you wrote to and when (kept up to 25 days). To force Apple to hand over what you actually wrote, police need a search warrant signed by a judge. With Advanced Data Protection turned on, a warrant no longer reaches your iCloud Backup, Photos, iCloud Drive or Notes: Apple doesn’t hold the keys. iCloud Mail, Contacts and Calendars aren’t covered, so a warrant still reaches them. An emergency request needs no judge at all, and Apple decides whether to answer it.

A ready-made kit clones the Google sign-in page. You type your password and code into the copy, and the operator uses both on the real page. Codes from a text or an app can be passed along like that; a passkey only answers Google’s real site.

a spyware vendor’s government customer (NSO Group’s Pegasus)
Security researchers traced Aurora to Elderwood, a Beijing-based group with ties to China’s military. NSO Group sells Pegasus to government agencies.

These go around the locks: into the phone or laptop itself, or into the company. The CIA’s phone and computer hacking tools were exposed in the Vault 7 leak (2017). In 2010 Google said the Aurora attackers had gone after the Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists. Google also said only two Gmail accounts appeared to have been accessed, and only their account information and subject lines, not the emails themselves. Citizen Lab has found Pegasus on the phones of journalists and activists.
Beyond your control. For people at higher risk, Google’s Advanced Protection Program requires a passkey or security key to sign in and is stricter about risky downloads.

Scout: “Much of this desk got easier to name after 2013, because of Edward. I think of him every time I draw it.”

Edward was an NSA contractor. In June 2013 he gave journalists, among them Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras and Ewen MacAskill, documents describing programs like PRISM, which collected data from the biggest email and cloud companies. The US charged him under the Espionage Act and revoked his passport. He has lived in exile in Russia ever since.
